title: Introduction to Furno
subtitle: Partimento foundations and the Rule of the Octave
description: Meet the Neapolitan partimento tradition, learn how figured-bass numbers work, and memorise the Rule of the Octave in major and minor — the harmonic map every later chapter builds on.

lessons.title: What is Partimento?
lessons.summary: A bass line as a complete lesson in composition.

content.title: A bass line that teaches
body: A partimento is a single written bass line, sometimes with a few numbers or a fragment of melody, that a student turns into complete music at the keyboard.

In the conservatories of eighteenth-century Naples, apprentices worked through hundreds of these basses. Each one quietly encoded a habit of good voice-leading, so that by playing them the student absorbed a whole musical vocabulary.
Think of a partimento less as a finished piece and more as a set of instructions: the bass tells you where the harmony is going, and your hands supply the rest.

content.prompt: What does a partimento usually give the player?
options: A fully written-out piece to be played exactly as notated
A bass line, sometimes with figures, to be realised into complete music
A melody with chord symbols written above it
A set of scales to be practised hands separately

answer.explanation: The core of a partimento is the bass. The player supplies harmony, voice-leading and often melody on top of it.

content.title: Who used partimenti?
body: Teachers in Naples — names such as Durante, Fenaroli and Furno appear in the surviving manuscripts — wrote graded collections of basses for their students.

Giovanni Furno's short method is a compact starting point: a handful of rules about which chords belong on which bass notes, followed by exercises that put those rules to work. This chapter follows that same spirit.

content.prompt: Partimento teaching flourished most famously in which city's conservatories?

answer.explanation: The Neapolitan conservatories were the great centre of partimento training in the eighteenth century.

content.prompt: Why did students play so many partimenti?
options: To build a memorised vocabulary of patterns they could improvise and compose with
To prepare for written theory examinations
To learn to sight-read difficult rhythms
Because printed music was forbidden in conservatories

answer.explanation: Repetition across many basses turned voice-leading patterns into reflexes — the raw material for improvisation and composition.

reviewItems.front: What is a partimento?
reviewItems.back: A (usually figured) bass line that the player realises into complete music at the keyboard.

reviewItems.front: Which city's conservatories made partimento training famous?

lessons.title: Recognize, Realize, Stylize
lessons.summary: Three stages for turning a bass into music.

content.title: A three-step habit
body: Working through any partimento can be split into three stages.
Recognize: look at the bass and identify the pattern — which scale degree are we on, which way is the line moving, is there a cadence coming?
Realize: choose the harmony that pattern calls for and place it under your fingers with smooth voice-leading.
Stylize: once the harmony is secure, decorate it — add figuration, imitation, or a melody — so the result sounds like real music rather than a chord exercise.

content.prompt: Put the three stages in the order you apply them.

answer.explanation: First identify the pattern, then supply its harmony, and only then decorate it.

content.prompt: You notice the bass is climbing step by step from the tonic. Which stage are you in?

answer.explanation: Identifying the shape of the bass is recognition — nothing has been played on top of it yet.

content.prompt: You turn plain block chords into a flowing broken-chord figure. Which stage is that?

answer.explanation: Adding figuration to harmony that is already in place is stylization.

content.prompt: Why is it risky to start stylizing before the harmony is secure?
options: Decoration makes the music too quiet
Elaborate figuration built on the wrong chords just makes wrong chords more noticeable
Stylizing is only allowed in fugues
There is no risk; order does not matter

answer.explanation: Stylization amplifies whatever is underneath it, so the harmonic skeleton has to be right first.

reviewItems.front: The three stages of working a partimento, in order?
In the three-stage process, what does 'Realize' mean?
reviewItems.back: Supplying the harmony the recognised pattern calls for, with good voice-leading.

lessons.title: Introduction to Figured Bass
lessons.summary: Reading the numbers: intervals above the bass.

content.title: Numbers are intervals
body: A figure is an interval counted upward from the bass note, using the notes of the key. A 6 means 'a sixth above the bass'; a 3 means 'a third above'.
Octaves don't matter: a tenth counts as a third, so you are free to place the upper notes wherever your hand is comfortable.
Figures are often abbreviated. A bass note with no figure normally means 5/3 (a root-position triad). A lone 6 means 6/3 — the third is understood.

content.prompt: In C major the bass is E with the figure 6. Which notes go above it?

answer.explanation: A third above E is G and a sixth above E is C, giving E–G–C: a C major chord in first inversion.

content.prompt: A bass note has no figure at all. What is normally assumed?

answer.explanation: An unfigured note is played as a root-position triad: a fifth and a third above the bass.

content.prompt: The bass is D with a 6. Play the note a sixth above D (in C major).

answer.explanation: Counting D(1)–E–F–G–A–B(6): a sixth above D is B.

content.prompt: Bass D, figures 6/4/3, in C major. Which set of upper notes matches?

answer.explanation: Third = F, fourth = G, sixth = B. Together with D that spells G–B–D–F: a dominant seventh with its fifth in the bass.

content.prompt: You place a note a tenth above the bass. How is it figured?

answer.explanation: Compound intervals reduce by an octave: a tenth is figured as a third.

reviewItems.front: An unfigured bass note normally implies which chord?
What does a lone '6' under a bass note stand for?
reviewItems.back: 6/3 — a sixth and a third above the bass (a first-inversion triad).

reviewItems.front: Bass D in C major, figure 6/4/3: which notes?
reviewItems.back: D with F, G and B (a G7 chord with D in the bass).

lessons.title: Rule of the Octave — Major
lessons.summary: One chord for every step of the scale, up and down.

content.title: A harmony for every scale step
body: The Rule of the Octave assigns a standard chord to each degree of a bass that moves by step through the scale. Learn it once and you can harmonise any stepwise bass on sight.
The stable degrees — 1 and 5 — take root-position triads. Most other degrees take sixth chords of some kind, which keeps the bass smooth and the harmony moving toward the next stable point.
Here is the ascending form in C major. Play it slowly and listen to how each chord leans toward the next.

content.prompt: Ascending in C major: which figure belongs on scale degree 2?

answer.explanation: Degree 2 takes 6/4/3 — a dominant-seventh sonority that leads naturally on to degree 3.

content.prompt: Ascending: what does the leading tone (degree 7) carry on its way to the octave?

answer.explanation: Degree 7 ascending takes 6/5 (B–D–F–G), another dominant-seventh shape that resolves to the tonic.

content.title: Coming back down
body: Descending, a few degrees change their chords. Degree 7 relaxes to a plain 6, degree 6 gets a raised sixth that points toward degree 5, and degree 4 takes 6/4/2 so its dissonance can fall to degree 3.
Here is the descending form in C major.

content.prompt: Which two scale degrees take a root-position 5/3 chord in both directions?

answer.explanation: Tonic and dominant are the stable pillars of the Rule of the Octave.

content.prompt: Degree 3 takes the same figure in both directions. Which?

answer.explanation: Degree 3 always carries a simple 6 — the tonic chord in first inversion.

content.prompt: Arrange the figures for degrees 1–4 ascending in major.

lessons.title: Rule of the Octave — Minor
lessons.summary: The same map in minor, with its characteristic colours.

content.title: Minor follows the same plan
body: In minor the chord types stay almost the same as in major, but the leading tone must be raised whenever dominant harmony appears. Figures with a sharp (♯) or natural (♮) remind you of that raised note.
Ascending, the bass itself usually raises degrees 6 and 7 so the line climbs smoothly to the tonic. Descending, the bass uses the natural (lowered) forms.
Here is the ascending form in A minor. Notice the G♯ and F♯ in the bass, and the ♯3 on degree 5.

content.prompt: In A minor, the bass reaches E (degree 5). What does the figure ♯ (or ♯3) tell you?
options: Raise the bass note to E♯
Play a major triad on E by raising the third to G♯
Play a minor triad on E
Add a sharp seventh above E

answer.explanation: A lone accidental applies to the third. E–G♯–B is the major dominant chord that minor keys need.

content.prompt: Play the leading tone of A minor — the note that degree 5's ♯3 creates.

answer.explanation: The leading tone of A minor is G♯, a half step below the tonic.

content.title: Descending in minor
body: Coming down, the bass returns to G♮ and F♮. Degree 6 (F) carries ♯6/4/3 — the raised sixth above F is D♯, producing a sharply directed chord that pushes into the dominant.
Degree 4 again takes 6/4/2, with a sharp on the fourth so the leading tone appears.

content.prompt: Ascending in A minor, which bass notes are usually raised?

answer.explanation: Degrees 6 and 7 rise to F♯ and G♯ so the bass climbs to the tonic without an augmented second.

content.prompt: Descending in A minor, the bass F carries ♯6/4/3. Play the raised sixth above F.

answer.explanation: A sixth above F in A minor is D; raising it gives D♯, which resolves up to E.

content.prompt: Degree 2 in minor (B in A minor) carries which figure, in either direction?

answer.explanation: Like major, degree 2 takes 6/4/3 — with the sixth raised to G♯ so the dominant has its leading tone.

reviewItems.front: Rule of the Octave, minor — degree 5?
reviewItems.back: 5/♯3 (major triad: raise the third to the leading tone).

reviewItems.front: Minor Rule of the Octave ascending: which bass degrees are raised?
reviewItems.back: Degrees 6 and 7 (e.g. F♯ and G♯ in A minor).

reviewItems.front: Minor Rule of the Octave descending — degree 6?
Minor Rule of the Octave — degree 2?
Minor Rule of the Octave descending — degree 4?

lessons.title: The 4–6 Exceptions
lessons.summary: Why degrees 4 and 6 change with direction.

content.title: Direction matters on 4 and 6
body: Most Rule of the Octave chords are the same whichever way the bass moves. Degrees 4 and 6 are the important exceptions — their chord depends on where the bass is heading.
Degree 4 going up to 5 takes 6/5. Degree 4 coming down from 5 takes 6/4/2: the bass note is now the dissonant seventh of a dominant chord, so it must keep falling to degree 3.
Degree 6 going up takes a plain 6. Degree 6 coming down to 5 takes ♯6/4/3, borrowing a leading tone that points at the dominant.

content.prompt: Bass F rising to G in C major. Which figure goes on F?

answer.explanation: Rising 4 → 5 takes 6/5 (F–A–C–D), a strong approach to the dominant.

content.prompt: Bass G falls to F, then to E. Which figure goes on F?

answer.explanation: Falling 5 → 4 → 3 takes 6/4/2 on F: G–B–D with F in the bass, resolving down to E.

content.prompt: Bass A falling to G in C major. Which figure goes on A?

answer.explanation: Descending 6 → 5 takes ♯6/4/3: A–C–D–F♯, which leans strongly into G.

content.prompt: In that ♯6/4/3 chord on A (C major), play the raised sixth.

answer.explanation: A sixth above A is F; raised, it becomes F♯ — the temporary leading tone to G.

content.prompt: Listen to the bass motion: the bass is on degree 6 and the next note is degree 7. Which chord does degree 6 take?

answer.explanation: Ascending, degree 6 is simply a 6 chord — the ♯6/4/3 only appears when the bass is falling to 5.

reviewItems.front: Degree 4 ascending (to 5) takes…
Degree 4 descending (from 5 to 3) takes…
reviewItems.back: 6/4/2 — the bass is a dissonant seventh that must fall.

reviewItems.front: Degree 6 ascending takes…
Degree 6 descending (to 5) takes…
reviewItems.back: ♯6/4/3 — a borrowed leading tone to the dominant.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 Practice & Review
lessons.summary: Mixed challenge across the whole chapter.

content.prompt: You have just decided that a stepwise bass calls for the Rule of the Octave. Which stage comes next?

answer.explanation: Recognition is done; now you realize the harmony.

content.prompt: Ascending major Rule of the Octave in G major: the bass is C (degree 4). Figure?

answer.explanation: Degree 4 rising to 5 takes 6/5 in every major key.

content.prompt: Arrange the figures for the major descending line 6 → 5 → 4 → 3.
In G major, play the bass note that always carries a root-position chord besides the tonic.

answer.explanation: The dominant of G major is D — degree 5 always takes 5/3.

content.prompt: In D minor, the bass descends B♭ → A. What does B♭ carry?

answer.explanation: Descending degree 6 to 5 takes ♯6/4/3 — here B♭–D–E–G♯.

content.prompt: Which statement about figures is true?
options: Figures are counted downward from the melody
A tenth must be written as 10
Unfigured notes are always left silent

answer.explanation: Figures count upward from the bass, compound intervals reduce, and a lone 6 implies 6/3.
